Traditional composite aircraft structures are designed with a no damage growth criterion requiring large knockdown factors to cover unknown effects.
The FAA introduced a slow growth approach in 2009 for certifying composite and adhesively bonded structures and bonded repairs.
Damage growth in composites often starts immediately upon loading and exhibits a near-exponential stable growth phase.
The lead crack concept, originally for metals, may be applicable to composite damage growth.
Experimental data reviewed include delamination and disbond growth in AS4/E7K8 and aluminium bonded joints under cyclic loading.
The strain energy release rate (SERR) is a key parameter correlating with delamination growth.
Paris law-based fatigue crack growth models have high exponents leading to large uncertainties in composites.
A modified Hartman-Schijve equation variant provides a better fit for fatigue crack growth in composites.
Parameters needed for damage tolerance assessment include loading spectrum, da/dN vs ΔG data, initial flaw size, critical ΔG values, and failure criteria.
Inspection programs under slow growth approach should specify frequency, extent, and methods of inspection.
Damage growth data are scarce and scattered, limiting the generalization of damage tolerance models.
Damage growth measurements used techniques like ultrasonic C-scanning and digital image correlation.
The lead crack growth framework can estimate conservative safe operational life after damage detection.
Environmental degradation and multi-site damage interactions remain open research questions.
The paper proposes a framework to apply the lead crack concept to composite aircraft structures to improve damage tolerance assessment.
The adhesive used in some tests was FM73 from Cytec.
Specimens tested included 20 mm wide bonded joints and 24-ply laminates with central holes.
Damage growth was monitored under various stress levels, e.g., 63%, 70%, 75% of design limit stress.
Damage growth data show scatter but generally conform to the lead crack growth pattern.
The slow growth approach could reduce unnecessary aircraft grounding and improve maintenance scheduling.
